If you’d like to play PS2 games on a tablet, the Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro can run God of War 2 at 60 frames per second and three times its original resolution. The Android tablet also gives you access to emulators through Google Play without sideloading. As reported by ETA Prime, GameCube and Wii games ran well too, although a couple of 3DS games crashed or had problems. See how the tablet handles games across different systems and why Vulkan was used for testing.

The Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro runs Android 16, providing Google Play access without sideloading. PS2 games generally ran well, with God of War 2 reaching 60 fps at 3× resolution and Shadow of the Colossus requiring native resolution. Three 3DS games ran at 2× resolution and 60 fps, but a couple crashed or failed to work correctly with Vulkan. PSP game God of War: Chains of Olympus ran at 4K, although the tablet’s display does not support 4K. Dolphin ran the demanding GameCube game F-Zero GX at 60 fps and 2× resolution, including on harder-to-emulate tracks.

The Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro runs Android 16 rather than Fire OS, so Google Play is available without sideloading for downloading emulators. Its MediaTek Dimensity 8400 and Mali-G720 MC7 GPU powered the emulators tested in tablet mode.

Its 11.95-inch IPS display has a 2800 × 1840 resolution and a 120Hz refresh rate. OpenGL would probably be fine for most emulation on Snapdragon devices, but ETA Prime recommends the Vulkan graphics backend for this MediaTek tablet. Vulkan was used instead of OpenGL throughout testing because of the Mali GPU.

PS2 games ran well, though the resolution varied by title. Gran Turismo 4 ran in NetherSX2 at 3.5× resolution, rendering at 2240 × 1568, while Ratchet & Clank: Going Commando looked excellent on the display at the same setting.

It was uncertain whether the frame-rate fluctuation in Need for Speed: Most Wanted was normal. Resident Evil 4 is locked to 30 fps on the original PS2, while Shadow of the Colossus needed the lower native resolution.

Learn more about retro emulation on tablets with other articles and guides we have written below.

Azahar ran several 3DS games at raised resolutions, but a couple of games crashed or failed to work correctly with its Vulkan backend. DOA Dimensions ran well through a couple of scenes at 2× resolution.

Mario Kart 7, Monster Hunter 4 Ultimate and Ridge Racer each ran at 2× and 60 fps. The Link Between Worlds was playable at 1.5×, with a Mali driver issue guessed to be a possible explanation for the lower setting.

God of War: Chains of Olympus ran at 4K, although the tablet’s display does not support 4K. Compatible PSP games should run at full speed.

Dolphin delivered strong results with the tested GameCube games. Auto Modellista ran at 60 fps at 4× resolution, or 2560 × 2112; it is a mid-range game to emulate.

The more demanding F-Zero GX held 60 fps at 2×, including on harder-to-emulate tracks. Metroid Prime was also tested at 3× resolution.

Wii games also ran really well in Dolphin. Tatsunoko vs. Capcom was tested at 4× resolution, while Smash Bros. for Wii and Mario Kart Wii were tested at 3×.

Before buying, we would check that the specific games you care about are reported to run well on this chip and graphics backend. A handful of titles in one video is a small sample, and results can differ between emulator versions.

ETA Prime calls the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro the best tablet Amazon has made, though it costs more than older Fire tablets. It suits players who want to emulate games across several systems, with many titles running at raised resolutions. It is a less certain fit for anyone expecting every 3DS game to work correctly: a couple crashed or had problems using Vulkan, and the lower resolution needed for The Link Between Worlds was guessed to be a Mali driver issue.

To complement the titanium frame, Apple may integrate curved glass, creating a seamless and robust design. This differentiation allows Apple to cater to a broader audience, offering a premium aesthetic for high-end models while maintaining a more traditional design for entry-level options. This approach underscores Apple’s focus on functionality over radical changes, making sure that the Dynamic Island remains a practical and intuitive feature. By improving its responsiveness and expanding its capabilities, Apple aims to make the Dynamic Island an indispensable part of the user experience, blending convenience with innovation.

Built using a 17-nanometer process, this sensor promises several key improvements, including faster readout speeds, enhanced HDR performance, reduced image distortion, and potentially lower power consumption. These advancements could significantly improve the quality of both photos and videos, making the device a compelling choice for photography enthusiasts.

While details about the sensor’s size and megapixel count remain undisclosed, the technology represents a substantial leap forward. Apple’s focus on professional-grade camera performance highlights its commitment to delivering a flagship device that excels in both everyday use and creative applications. This upgrade could further solidify the iPhone’s reputation as a leader in mobile photography.

Apple is reportedly developing four distinct models for the iPhone 20 lineup, with design variations playing a key role in differentiating the offerings. The Pro models are expected to feature curved glass, while the standard versions may retain a flat glass design. This strategy allows Apple to cater to a wide range of user preferences, offering premium features for those seeking innovative design and more traditional options for users who value simplicity.

Additionally, the flat glass design could serve as a contingency plan if production challenges arise with the curved glass prototypes. By maintaining flexibility in its manufacturing process, Apple ensures that it can meet demand while minimizing potential delays. This approach reflects Apple’s ability to adapt to market needs without compromising on quality or innovation.

As Apple continues to test various prototypes, the iPhone 20 Pro Max represents a thoughtful blend of innovation and legacy. The potential reintroduction of titanium frames, the refinement of the Dynamic Island, and the adoption of advanced camera technology all demonstrate Apple’s willingness to revisit past designs while pushing the boundaries of what a smartphone can achieve.

Some long-standing features may be reimagined or even removed entirely, reflecting Apple’s commitment to evolving its products in response to user feedback and technological advancements. Whether these changes will resonate with consumers or spark debate remains to be seen, but they underscore Apple’s dedication to delivering a device that balances tradition with progress.

The iPhone 20 Pro Max represents a bold step forward for Apple, combining nostalgic design elements with state-of-the-art technology. From the potential use of titanium frames to the refinement of the Dynamic Island and the introduction of a new camera sensor, the device promises to deliver a unique blend of durability, performance, and style. A health-age score sounds simple: the younger the number, the healthier you are. It is less simple than that, because two scores can be answering different questions. Google Health Age focuses on heart and metabolic risk, while Whoop Age takes a broader view of health span. Google’s main score can show you at most 3.29 years younger, while a Whoop result shown by The Quantified Scientist was 13.1 years younger using a different calculation. Whoop Age is available now, while Google’s score remains a research project with no current release plan. Get the details on what each score measures and where its limits lie.

Google’s Health Age is an unreviewed research project, and Google says it has no current plan to offer it as a feature. Google’s score focuses on cardiometabolic disease risk, while Whoop Age focuses more broadly on health span and mortality. Google’s core score can reduce calculated age by at most about 3.29 years below chronological age. Google’s Sensor WM uses two weeks of wearable data to predict measurements over the following 12 weeks, but its observational training cannot prove causation. Participants whose health age exceeded their chronological age had approximately 3% lower estimated cardiometabolic disease-free survival over the following year.

Google’s Health Age and Whoop Age turn changeable health factors into a number expressed in years, but focus on different outcomes. Google’s research centers on cardiometabolic disease, meaning conditions of the heart and metabolism such as heart disease and type 2 diabetes. Whoop Age is framed more broadly around health span and lifestyle factors associated with mortality.

Google calls its metric coachable health age. It is a research project described in a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, not an active feature. Google says it currently has no plan to include it as a feature, and the code is expected to be released only after journal acceptance. A health-age feature is something Google is still missing, while most of its competitors already have one.

Health Age is a risk score expressed as an age; it does not directly measure how old your cells are. Google’s researchers designed it around wearable measurements people can influence, rather than factors such as genetics or family history.

Its core calculation uses resting heart rate, average daily steps, sleep duration and weekly active zone minutes. Evidence links those inputs to outcomes including cardiovascular disease, heart failure and type 2 diabetes.

The model weights those risk factors, converts their contributions into equivalent years and adds or subtracts the difference from chronological age. The weights come from hazard ratios, which are figures from published studies showing how much a factor raises or lowers the risk of disease. Optional inputs include estimated cardiorespiratory fitness, sleep regularity and predicted insulin resistance. Google also tries to account for correlations between inputs, such as the possible overlap between steps and active minutes.

Learn more about Google and Whoop health metrics with other articles and guides we have written below.

For resting heart rate, steps and sleep duration, the core model uses fixed reference values rather than personal targets. A resting heart rate of 60 beats per minute or lower adds nothing to the score, while sleeping between six and nine hours leaves it unchanged.

More than 8,000 daily steps can lower the score, but the reduction stops at 9,000, so taking 20,000 steps does not lower the core score further. Weekly active zone minutes begin reducing the score at 115 minutes, and going beyond about 500 brings no further reduction.

Those limits prevent the calculation from producing an indefinitely younger age through extreme amounts of activity. In the main version Google presents, the largest reduction is about 3.29 years below chronological age.

The Quantified Scientist warns that a relatively active person could reach the maximum reduction quickly and lose motivation, even if further health gains are possible. A static calculation can struggle to model physiological adaptation and interactions among factors. Optional measurements might address some of the simplicity, although adding them would not automatically make Google’s approach better.

Like Google’s score, Whoop Age connects changeable behaviors and physiological signals to risk estimates and is designed for actionability rather than simply predicting chronological age, but it draws on more components. Whoop also attempts to account for correlations between variables. The Whoop app lists contributors including sleep consistency and duration, strain, heart-rate zones, strength activity, steps, VO2 max, resting heart rate and lean body mass.

Whoop’s health span score mainly uses research connecting lifestyle factors with the risk of dying later in life. Google’s score instead places more emphasis on the earlier development of conditions such as heart disease, heart failure, hypertension and type 2 diabetes.

In simplified terms, Google’s score focuses more on nearer-term heart health, while Whoop’s focuses more on longer-term health span and all-cause mortality, the risk of dying from any cause. Combining hazard ratios from different studies and disease outcomes creates its own assumptions.

In our view, the number matters less than the question behind it. One score estimates nearer-term heart and metabolic risk, while the other estimates long-term mortality, so being “younger” on one does not mean the same thing as on the other.

The Quantified Scientist’s own Whoop app displayed an age 13.1 years younger. That result and Google’s maximum reduction of 3.29 years come from different calculations, so the two figures cannot be set side by side.

Alongside the score, Google describes a model it calls the sensor world model, or Sensor WM. It uses two weeks of wearable data to predict measurements over the following 12 weeks, compares a change in habits with continuing the same routine, and ranks actions such as walking, sleeping or doing more cardio by how much they could improve Health Age and how realistic they are. An AI coach communicates the result.

In Google’s testing, Sensor WM performed well for resting heart rate, heart-rate variability and breathing rate. Because the model was trained on observational data without interventions, it cannot prove causation: diet, medication, stress and other changes may confound the results.

Google’s researchers compared coachable Health Age with established cardiometabolic measures. They reported an absolute correlation of 0.512 with a modified version of the American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 score, on a scale where 0 means no relationship and 1 a perfect match. The score also correlated with a metabolic syndrome severity score.

Participants’ calculated health ages also became progressively older as they rated their own health from excellent toward poor. Those relationships suggest the score captures information relevant to current cardiometabolic health, although some analyses have confounders.

In another analysis, the researchers combined Fitbit data with electronic health records for tens of thousands of people. The wearable score added a small amount of information for predicting who would stay free of disease. Participants whose health age exceeded their chronological age had lower estimated cardiometabolic disease-free survival over the following year, with a difference of approximately 3%.

For now, Whoop Age is the one you can actually use, since Google’s score remains research with no current plan to release it. The Quantified Scientist recommends Whoop Age for people particularly interested in athletic performance and health tracking, because its added factors offer more ways to improve, and thinks both approaches could be good while wishing Google’s allowed a greater reduction in age. Which approach leads to healthier, longer lives is not yet known; that would take long-term studies. If you already wear a Whoop band, its age score is well worth a look, as long as you read it as one view of your health and not the whole picture.

Can you print full-color 3D models without painting them by hand? The new Flashforge CJ270 does just that, and is currently on offer at $3,999 in the United States and £3,499 in the United Kingdom. It’s a desktop resin printer that builds color and detail into each layer, while its water-soluble supports hold complex shapes in place during printing. Flashforge says it can produce more than 10 million color combinations, although the finished models can be brittle. Find out how the printing and cleanup work, as well as what Uncle Jessy found when using the CJ270.

The Flashforge CJ270 is on offer at $3,999 in the United States (regular price $4,499) and £3,499 in the United Kingdom (regular price £3,999). Flashforge says the printer can produce more than 10 million color combinations using MultiJet Printing. Its build volume is 180 × 120 × 100 mm, with a layer thickness of 7 micrometers. Flashforge says models under 10 cm may print in less than 10 hours, depending on their dimensions and orientation. Prints can be brittle, and parts of a Skull Kid model snapped after a drop of about one foot.

The Flashforge CJ270 is a desktop 3D printer that uses inkjet-style printing rather than a single vat of resin. Flashforge announced it in September 2026 and says it can produce more than 10 million color combinations.

Unlike UV printers that produce flat or raised-surface images, the CJ270 makes three-dimensional objects. It is currently priced under $4,000 in the United States, while Flashforge puts the price of traditional industrial full-color 3D printers at approximately $150,000. Some competitors cost roughly $50,000 to $100,000 or more.

The CJ270 uses MultiJet Printing to deposit droplets of photosensitive resin, then cures them with ultraviolet light. Seven printheads handle cyan, magenta, yellow, black, white, clear and support materials, while a roller levels each layer before curing.

Color, structure and supports are built together. Depending on the settings, the printer can use color on an object’s exterior and white for its solid interior. Clear resin can replace white infill for a translucent appearance, although colors were harder to see on a mimic chest printed that way.

A textured magnetic PEI build plate and automatic leveling are included, and prints made so far required no ink calibration. The CJ270’s build volume is only slightly smaller than that of a larger Mimaki printer. Its main specifications are:

Flashforge claims traditional industrial full-color printers use layers of approximately 20-30 micrometers and that the CJ270 occupies less than one-twentieth of their size. Its noise is comparable to that of typical FDM printers: it is audible in the same room but not noticeably audible from another room. An activated-carbon air filter is included, and a fan runs whenever the printer is powered on, including while idle.

Here are additional guides from our expansive article library that you may find useful on 3D printing.

A CJ270 model included colors, shading and small details directly in the print, without hand painting. A small goblin head also captured color variations and details, though its metallic areas did not stand out as strongly.

Water-soluble supports hold overhangs and complex shapes and can fully encase a model. A multicolored Skull Kid model had many overhangs, while a mimic model combined recessed areas and overhangs that would have been difficult to prepare for hand painting with an FDM or resin printer. Comparable resin printing could also leave many support scars to clean up.

Prints can be brittle, depending on their size and thickness. A thin shovel piece broke repeatedly, and parts of the Skull Kid print snapped after a drop of about a foot. Flashforge does not recommend CJ270 models for load-bearing parts or functional prototypes under significant mechanical stress.

A print job containing an Aztec dragon partially failed, although the dragon itself was cleaned up. Another mimic print failed and affected nearby models on the build plate.

Flashforge ColorPrint lets you arrange, rotate and scale models, manage supports and layouts, and control the cyan, magenta, yellow, black, white and clear material channels independently. It estimates jobs before slicing and shows ink usage. Time estimates are reportedly close but not exact, and sending a job to the printer can take time depending on model complexity.

A library of downloadable full-color models is included. Finding full-color files elsewhere was the biggest challenge with the printer, and most models imported in the GLB format needed rescaling.

ColorPrint supports CJP, CJM, STL, OBJ, 3MF, STEP, STP, PLY, FBX, GLB, GLTF and WRL files. Version 1.6.1 is available for 64-bit Windows, Intel macOS and Apple Silicon macOS; Flashforge also lists CJ270 firmware version 2.8.4.

Flashforge says models under 10 cm may print in less than 10 hours, depending on their dimensions and orientation. Adding models may increase print time only slightly if they remain within similar X, Y and Z constraints. Flashforge estimates about 15 hours or more for models around 10 cm and 25 hours or more for those around 15 cm.

Print files can reach the CJ270 over a wired local network or by USB drive. Wi-Fi is not currently supported, although Flashforge says support is planned for later in 2026.

For a wired connection, the touchscreen displays the printer’s IP address and DNS information for computer configuration. The USB port and touchscreen are on the front left, the RFID reader is opposite, and the Ethernet port, power cable and switch are on the back. The one-time setup was complicated, and a Mac without an Ethernet port also needs an adapter.

After a print finishes, the touchscreen does not display the actual time taken. Flashforge is reportedly working on an update for that display.

The CJ270 currently accepts only Flashforge’s dedicated materials, sold in 100 g pouches individually or in combinations, with bulk ink pricing also available. When scanned, a single-activation RFID card transfers the authorized material balance to the printer. Resin can be added during a print without pausing it.

A card failed to scan on a rare occasion in Uncle Jessy’s use. The printer also purges ink into a waste tank during printing, preparation and cleaning, so the tank needs periodic attention; it is opposite the ink-loading panel.

Unopened resin has a stated shelf life of 18 months, and Flashforge recommends using it within two months of opening. The company advises wearing nitrile gloves when handling resin and keeping products out of children’s reach. Uncle Jessy recommends ventilation while the printer is operating, even though no strong odor was noticed in the workshop or while the printer was idle.

Finished objects can be lifted from the build plate and soaked in water to remove supports. Flush cutters are useful for removing excess support first, and water agitation helps with removal. Excess residue can be scraped off the build plate before another print. Flashforge says no separate post-curing step is needed; sanding, polishing and gloss coating are optional.

Prints are porous and can absorb considerable clear-coat spray, so they may need multiple coats depending on the desired finish. Matte, gloss and semigloss clear coats can be used, and a small wire brush can remove flashing.

An ultrasonic cleaner can assist with support removal, which Flashforge claims it can reduce from around 10 hours to one to two hours. For the models tested, cleanup with an ultrasonic cleaner or resin wash station took roughly one to two hours, depending on size and recessed areas. The amount of support also affected cleanup time, and no major print-quality difference was noticed between the methods for those models.

Cleaning tanks can accumulate slight residue at the bottom. Uncle Jessy recommends collecting dirty wash water rather than pouring it down the drain; disposal rules may vary by location.

The touchscreen prompts users to clean the printheads and roller and empty the waste tank before, during or after print jobs. Each printhead can be replaced individually. Flashforge claims a service life of up to 2,000 operating hours and estimates that printheads may last up to a year with proper maintenance, depending on usage.

Flashforge provides maintenance guides and videos for part replacement and machine jobs. The printer carries a 12-month limited warranty, while the printheads have a three-month warranty.

What stands out to us is the color itself. Shading, gradients and fine detail come out of the machine already in the model, which removes hand painting from the process altogether, and until recently that kind of printing belonged to industrial systems costing many times more. Uncle Jessy’s prints show what that looks like in practice better than a specification sheet can. The caution is in the running of it: the CJ270 only accepts Flashforge’s own resin, loaded with single-use cards, so the cost of ownership will depend on how much you print.

At the time of writing, the CJ270 is on offer at $3,999 in the United States and £3,499 in the United Kingdom, down from regular prices of $4,499 and £3,999. Flashforge sells it through both countries’ online stores and says new and remaining orders are scheduled to ship by air in the next batch at the end of November 2026. Printing requires the dedicated resin and ColorPrint software.

Full color on a desk for under $4,000 is a fraction of the price of the industrial machines that came before it. If you want finished-looking models without picking up a paintbrush, the CJ270 is well worth a look, as long as you can live with fragile prints and a wired connection for now.

Checking the air quality at the end of your garden, or a kilometer down the road, normally means running power and Wi-Fi out to wherever the sensor sits. This solar-powered ESP32 project needs neither: it sent readings from almost one kilometer away using LoRa radio, with a solar panel and battery keeping it running through the night. How To Electronics shows how the sensors and radio boards fit together, as well as how to view and save the readings from a dashboard on your phone or computer.

Two ESP32-S3 boards link an outdoor sensor station to an indoor dashboard over LoRa, so the outdoor unit needs no Wi-Fi. The PMS7003 measures PM1.0, PM2.5 and PM10, while the BME680 measures temperature, humidity, pressure and gas resistance. The outdoor ESP32-S3 passes sensor data to its LoRa radio approximately every 15 seconds. A solar panel charges the outdoor transmitter’s 3.7 V, 5,200 mAh battery, which powers it when the panel is not generating power. The indoor receiver connects to local Wi-Fi and hosts a dashboard that saves readings in flash storage and exports them as CSV files.

This solar-powered LoRa air quality monitor uses two custom ESP32-S3 boards: one collects readings outdoors, while the other receives them indoors and hosts a local dashboard. In the test, the outdoor unit was placed almost one kilometer from home and its readings were viewed on a computer, although the dashboard can also be opened on a smartphone or tablet. What stands out to us is the range. Most home air quality monitors only tell you about the room they sit in, so being able to read one almost a kilometer away opens up uses that a Wi-Fi sensor simply cannot cover.

The transmitter combines a particulate sensor and an environmental sensor. The Plantower PMS7003 uses laser scattering to measure PM1.0, PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations in µg/m³, while the BME680 measures temperature, humidity, pressure and gas resistance.

Bosch BSEC2 processes the BME680 data to produce an Indoor Air Quality (IAQ) index and estimated CO₂-equivalent and VOC-equivalent readings. An ESP32-S3 collects the data and passes it to the LoRa radio approximately every 15 seconds.

Become an expert in LoRa and air quality with the help of our in-depth articles and helpful guides.

The custom transmitter board has an I²C header for the BME680 and a UART header for the PMS7003. Extra GPIO headers support additional sensors, and a connector accepts the solar panel.

On the board, the BQ25185 manages solar and USB charging, with reverse-polarity protection at the battery connection. A 5 V boost converter supplies power when the microcontroller signals it, while a separate buck converter provides 3.3 V.

For charging and code uploads, the transmitter has a USB-C port connected through a CP2104 USB-to-UART converter. The battery capacity was chosen to keep the unit running overnight, when the solar panel cannot supply power.

The receiver uses the same LoRa module and another ESP32-S3, but it does not need external environmental sensors. Connect its antenna and rechargeable lithium-ion battery to complete the basic hardware.

Its MCP73831 charger handles battery charging without a solar input, and a buck-boost converter supplies 3.3 V. The receiver also has reverse-polarity protection, an autoprogrammer and a reset section.

Both boards were designed as custom PCBs in EasyEDA, with placement and routing based on component data-sheet guidance. A PCB service assembled the boards.

The firmware uses the Arduino IDE, RadioLib for LoRa communication and Bosch BSEC2 for environmental processing. The transmitter code separates the two sensor readings and sends them to the receiver. Its low-power mode turns off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth and runs the CPU at 80 MHz.

Because the PMS7003 fan must remain on, the transmitter cannot enter deep sleep. To upload the code, select the ESP32-S3 dev module and the correct COM port, then connect the transmitter to the computer by USB-C.

In the receiver code, change the Wi-Fi SSID and password before uploading. Select the same board type and the appropriate COM port, then use an FTDI module through the programming header: the receiver’s USB-C port is for charging only. The receiver’s dashboard.h file contains the HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the web page.

Place the transmitter outdoors with its sensors, battery and solar panel. After you switch on the transmitter and power the receiver indoors, the receiver connects to the configured Wi-Fi network.

In the receiver’s serial monitor, you can see incoming readings, signal strength, acknowledgements and its local IP address. RSSI and SNR readings also provide information about the radio link. Open the IP address in a browser to reach the dashboard.

On the dashboard, the overview shows an IAQ gauge alongside PM2.5, PM10, temperature, humidity and estimated CO₂- and VOC-equivalent values, with graphs over time. The environment page adds altitude, dew point, vapor pressure, air density and heat index, plus separate temperature, humidity and pressure graphs.

The air quality page shows historical IAQ and estimated gas-equivalent trends. The particulate page displays PM1.0, PM2.5 and PM10, a combined graph and a particle-size distribution chart. Settings include alert thresholds for air quality and particulate matter, as well as light and dark themes.

Readings are automatically saved in the receiver’s LittleFS flash storage, which retains the history after a restart. The data logger displays timestamps, lets you select parameters and exports a CSV file for later analysis.

Circuit diagrams, PCB design files, source code, wiring details and setup instructions have been published with the project, so you can build it as shown or adapt it to your own needs.

The spare GPIO headers on the outdoor board leave room to add other sensors later, giving you a way to grow the station beyond the original build. For anyone who wants to keep an eye on outdoor air quality from indoors, this solar-powered LoRa air quality monitor is an ESP32 project well worth building.

The Samsung Galaxy S27 Ultra introduces a blend of advancements and compromises, offering a refined flagship experience while sparking debate among tech enthusiasts. With a higher rumored price point, improved battery capacity, and a redesigned aesthetic, it aims to push the boundaries of premium smartphones ahead of its expected early 2027 debut. However, the rumored removal of the dedicated 3x telephoto lens and limited upgrades in certain areas may leave some questioning whether it’s a worthwhile leap from the S26 Ultra.

5,700 mAh Silicon-Carbon Boost: Breaks Samsung’s long-standing 5,000 mAh ceiling with a 14% capacity jump paired with a more efficient M16 OLED panel. The 3x Telephoto Catch: Rumors indicate Samsung is dropping the dedicated 10MP 3x zoom lens, relying on sensor cropping from a new 200MP ISOCELL HP6 primary camera instead. Wide Camera Bar & Privacy Display 2: Replaces individual floating lens rings with a horizontal camera plateau while adding native DC dimming and smarter Privacy Display controls. Steeper Price Tag: Tipped to start around $1,499—up from the S26 Ultra’s $1,299.99 launch price (and $100 above its post-October $1,399.99 tag).

One of the most noticeable differences between the S27 Ultra and its predecessor is the price. Rumored to start at $1,499 in the US, the S27 Ultra sits $200 above the S26 Ultra’s original $1,299.99 launch price—and $100 higher than its post-October $1,399.99 adjusted retail tag (with steeper jumps when factoring in discounted S26 Ultra street deals). This increase reflects rising component costs alongside the integration of technologies such as the M16 OLED display and 2nm silicon. While these enhancements are appealing, the higher entry price raises a critical question: do the upgrades justify the additional cost? For current S26 Ultra owners, the answer depends heavily on how much they value extra endurance and display refinements.

The S27 Ultra delivers a long-awaited jump in battery capacity, moving to a rumored 5,700 mAh silicon-carbon cell—a 14% increase over the 5,000 mAh pack used across the S26 Ultra and six prior Ultra generations. Combined with the energy-efficient M16 OLED display and 2nm chipset efficiency, this upgrade promises noticeably longer screen-on endurance for power users. Although wired charging speeds remain capped at 60W alongside 25W Qi2 magnetic wireless charging, Samsung is expected to maintain steady charging curves over extended sessions. For users who found the S26 Ultra’s battery life adequate, this upgrade may feel evolutionary, but it’s a welcome breakthrough for heavy travelers and gamers.

The camera system on the S27 Ultra introduces both advancements and compromises. Moving from a quad-camera array down to a triple-lens setup, the removal of the dedicated 10MP 3x telephoto lens marks a major shift, with Samsung relying on high-resolution in-sensor cropping from a new 200MP ISOCELL HP6 main sensor alongside a 50MP ultrawide and 50MP 5x periscope zoom. The updated primary sensor is designed to capture cleaner light and wider dynamic range, particularly in tricky contrast, while the front camera is also tipped to step up to 16MP. Still, the absence of a dedicated 3x optical lens raises valid questions about mid-range zoom consistency in dim lighting—a potential trade-off for portrait shooters.

The S27 Ultra debuts a bold visual shift, replacing the individual floating camera rings of the S26 Ultra with a wide horizontal camera plateau. This cleaner bar layout helps reduce table wobble when the phone rests flat and frees up internal room for native magnetic Qi2 alignment. However, this redesign comes with an immediate practical drawback: older cases are completely incompatible, requiring upgraders to replace their existing protective covers and accessories. While the refreshed rear aesthetic aligns the Ultra with the rumored Galaxy S27 Pro, longtime fans may need time to warm up to the departure from Samsung’s signature ring silhouette.

The 6.9-inch QHD+ display remains one of the S27 Ultra’s strongest assets. It introduces Privacy Display Version 2 with smarter directional viewing controls for split-screen apps and sensitive notifications, catering to commuters and multitaskers. Upgrading from the S26 Ultra’s M14 panel to Samsung’s new M16 OLED material brings higher peak efficiency and lower power draw. Additionally, the inclusion of native DC dimming helps reduce low-brightness PWM flicker, making the screen noticeably gentler on sensitive eyes. For buyers who prioritize display comfort and privacy, this panel represents a meaningful step forward.

The S27 Ultra is powered by Qualcomm’s 2nm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor (with Samsung’s Exynos 2700 also rumored for select markets), paired with faster LPDDR6 RAM and UFS 5.0/5.1 storage. This hardware delivers faster graphics and stronger on-device AI throughput for demanding games and creative workflows. The device also launches with Android 17 and One UI 9.5, introducing native App Lock, upgraded Expert RAW controls, and smarter Bixby automation. While many One UI 9.5 features will roll out to the S26 Ultra via software updates, the S27 Ultra’s 2nm silicon and memory bandwidth give it extra headroom.

For owners of older flagships like the Galaxy S24 Ultra or S25 Ultra, the S27 Ultra’s 5,700 mAh battery, M16 OLED panel, and 2nm chipset add up to a substantial generational leap. However, for current S26 Ultra owners, the calculus is far tighter. Core traits like the 6.9-inch screen size, 60W wired charging, and S Pen functionality carry over largely intact, while the higher rumored $1,499 price tag and dropped 3x lens introduce real trade-offs. Unless longer battery endurance and Privacy Display 2 sit at the top of your wishlist, holding onto the S26 Ultra remains a smart move.

The Samsung Galaxy S27 Ultra strikes a careful balance between hardware ambition and everyday practicality, delivering welcome gains in battery capacity, display efficiency, and processing speed. Yet the removal of the dedicated 3x telephoto lens and a steeper starting price ensure it won’t be an automatic upgrade for everyone. Weighing those camera and pricing catches against its battery and screen upgrades will make it clear which Ultra belongs in your pocket.

Turning a rough sketch into a mechanical design that actually moves normally means working through several different tools, from CAD software to simulation code. OpenAI’s new GPT-6.2 Astra can now handle that whole chain itself, producing the parts, the maths behind their movement and a 3D scene that shows the mechanism running. Discover how the model built a complete pendulum clock design from a single request, how it compares with rival models on 3D work, and what you still need to check before sending a design to your printer.

GPT-6.2 Astra produced a full pendulum clock design from a sketch, with every part modelled in CAD. It wrote its own Python solver to calculate and simulate how the mechanism moves. A Blender scene showed the gears running, alongside an exploded view and assembly instructions. OpenAI claims a score of 1,318 Elo for interactive 3D work, ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 on 1,271. The clock has not been printed or physically tested, so the design still needs checking.

Released on November 17, 2026, GPT-6.2 Astra is OpenAI’s successor to GPT-6 Astra, a reasoning model aimed at professional work, coding and scientific research. It accepts text and images and can use tools to run code and operate software, which is what makes a multi-step engineering job like this possible in a single session.

The request was simple to describe and demanding to carry out: design a 3D-printable pendulum clock. Astra began with a sketch, then modelled each component individually in CAD. A mechanical clock is a useful test because nothing works unless everything works. The gears have to mesh, the parts have to fit, and the whole assembly has to be something a person could put together.

The model produced three things you would expect from a human designer:

A static model only tells you what a design looks like. To show how it behaves, Astra wrote a Python solver to calculate and simulate the motion of the mechanical parts, then generated charts and graphs from the results.

This is the step that separates a 3D picture from a piece of engineering. The model was not only drawing shapes that resemble a clock. It was working out how the mechanism should move and producing evidence you can inspect, which gives you something to check before any plastic is used.

For the final stage, Astra built a Blender environment where the clock could be viewed in 3D with its gears in motion. Seeing the mechanism run makes problems far easier to spot than reading a parts list, and it gives anyone following the assembly instructions a clear picture of what the finished clock should do.

Taken together, the workflow covers the full path from idea to a design that is ready for testing: sketch, CAD parts, exploded view, instructions, simulation and a moving 3D visualization.

Learn more about GPT-6 Astra by reading our previous articles, guides and features :

OpenAI claims a score of 1,318 Elo on the AA-3D benchmark for interactive 3D work, compared with 1,271 for Claude Fable 5.2. That is the company’s own figure, but it matches what the clock demonstration suggests: 3D modelling is one of the areas where the new model is strongest.

The results are not flawless. In a separate test, Astra created 3D player shapes for a bot-fighting game. They were an improvement on what earlier models produced, yet the finished shapes still did not look good. Mechanical parts with clear rules appear to suit the model better than characters that need to look right to the eye.

The most important caveat is a practical one. The pendulum clock has not been 3D-printed or physically tested. A simulation showing gears turning is a strong starting point, but it is not proof that a printed mechanism will run smoothly or keep accurate time. Tolerances, friction and the strength of printed parts only show up on the workbench.

If you want to try this kind of project yourself, treat the output as a first draft from a capable assistant:

Wes Roth points to 3D modelling as the area where Astra excels, while noting that other models may still be the better choice for coding.

If you design mechanical parts for 3D printing and want to move from sketch to a simulated, viewable design much faster, the new GPT-6.2 Astra is well worth exploring in more detail.

If you want your living room lights to respond to where people are, the Aqara FP400 can detect presence and divide an open room into zones, even when someone is sitting still. Smart Life shows how the radar sensor works with Home Assistant to control lights and wake a dashboard, while custom zones require setup in Aqara Home and a compatible hub. Here is how the zones work, what reaches Home Assistant and why placement matters when covering a living and dining area.

The Aqara FP400 uses 60 GHz radar to detect people, including those sitting still, without capturing images. It divides a room into up to eight custom zones on a 0.5 m × 0.5 m grid for location-based automations. Aqara says the FP400 can track up to 10 people at once, while testing demonstrated separate tracking of two people. Custom zones in Home Assistant require Aqara Home setup and a compatible hub, while direct Thread provides only whole-room presence and light readings. The FP400 requires constant USB-C power and careful placement within its 120° detection angle.

The FP400 is a radar sensor that works out where people are in a room, not only whether someone is there, and it does so without a camera. In a combined living and dining area, testing found the zones more useful for automations than the ability to track a large group.

The FP400 can divide a room into up to eight custom zones using a 0.5 m × 0.5 m grid. In testing, three zones covered a living area, a dining area and the space directly in front of a Home Assistant display.

Those zones can control different lights according to where someone is sitting. The FP400 also measures light, so an automation can turn on lights only when the room is dark enough.

Aqara says the sensor can track up to 10 people at once. In testing, the Aqara Home map showed a position moving around the room and tracked two people separately, while a counter showed how many people the sensor detected.

Below are more guides on smart home tech and Home Assistant from our extensive range of articles.

The FP400 supports both Zigbee and Matter over Thread, but the zones are only available once the sensor has been set up in the Aqara Home app through an Aqara hub. That needs Aqara Home 6.4.1 or later and hub firmware 4.5.70 or later, on one of these hubs:

The Hub M2, M1S, M1S Gen 2 and E1 are not supported, nor are the Camera Hub G3, G2H and G2H Pro, and Aqara notes that availability varies by region and firmware. In testing, an older M2 could not be used, so the sensor was connected by Zigbee to the hub built into a G410 doorbell’s indoor chime.

A direct Thread connection to Home Assistant, without Aqara Home, gives you basic presence detection and the light sensor but no custom zones. Aqara strongly discourages that route, because it limits the FP400 to a single whole-area occupancy sensor. Using it on any third-party Matter platform also requires a Matter controller and a Thread border router that the platform supports.

Once the sensor is connected, you can create a room map, draw zones and adjust detection settings in Aqara Home, then use a Matter pairing code generated in the app to share the supported capabilities with another platform. In testing, the G410 acted as that Matter bridge to Home Assistant.

The connection exposed all three configured zones, whole-room presence and the light level in lux, which was enough for the tested automations. The live tracking map and the people count remained in Aqara Home.

Home Assistant can combine the FP400 with devices from different brands. A cinema-mode automation can close smart shades and dim lights when someone is in the living-area zone and a connected TV starts playback, and the sensor’s brightness reading can decide whether the shades need to close at all.

A smaller zone can make a display respond only when someone approaches it. In testing, an automation checked whether a person had stood in the zone for two seconds, then changed the display from a clock screensaver to the Home Assistant dashboard without a touch, returning to the clock after the person left. Because the zone was small, the dashboard did not wake every time someone walked through the room.

The FP400 is small, with a magnetic mount that lets you adjust its angle, and it needs a constant USB-C power connection, which limits where it can go. Its 120° detection angle makes placement important when one sensor has to cover both a living and a dining area.

Inside is a 60 GHz mmWave radar with a 4T4R MIMO antenna array, which is what lets it detect someone who is not moving. Aqara claims the array captures more than five times as much point-cloud data as its previous generation, and that its AI sensing adapts to the surrounding space over time.

An AI person-detection feature is designed to tell people apart from pets and robot vacuums, reducing false triggers. Smart Life recommends adjusting sensitivity and detection times to suit the room.

The Aqara FP300 runs on batteries and combines PIR and radar sensing with temperature, humidity and light measurements. The FP400 gives up the battery along with temperature and humidity, and in return adds people tracking and zones. A 15% Black Friday discount on the FP400 was available when the video was published.

Smart Life would still pick the FP300 for a bedroom and would not put an FP400 in every room, but for a large open space where one sensor can drive several automations, the FP400 is the one that makes sense. Check your hub against the supported list before buying, since that decides whether you get the zones at all.

Google has not announced a Pixel 12 series, yet early GSMA database listings and supply-chain leaks pointing to an August 2027 launch window outline a familiar four-model lineup: Pixel 12, Pixel 12 Pro, Pixel 12 Pro XL, and Pixel 12 Pro Fold. Subtle Slab Shifts & Fold Boost: The three non-foldable models show slight vertical pixel trims compared with Pixel 11 counterparts, while the Pixel 12 Pro Fold’s inner screen jumps to 2,296 × 2,404—a roughly 24% pixel increase. Rather than streamlining its hardware portfolio, Google appears committed to maintaining a four-device core structure for its 2027 flagship generation, pairing three conventional slab phones with one book-style foldable:

While a budget-focused Pixel 12a remains a recurring possibility later in the 2027–2028 cycle, early database entries confirm that Google’s primary August launch focus remains centered on these four flagship tiers.

Google continues its long-running tradition of assigning thematic internal codenames—this time centered on primates—alongside distinct hardware model numbers registered in early GSMA IMEI database entries:

These identifiers help track early certification filings, benchmark runs, and carrier testing well before official marketing names appear. Following Google’s naming pattern by physical scale, “Silverback” designates the largest slab flagship while “Capuchin” identifies the folding model.

The most concrete specifications surfaced so far involve exact display resolutions across all four devices. Comparing the leaked Pixel 12 figures against the Pixel 11 lineup reveals two distinct display strategies:

On the three conventional slab models, horizontal pixel counts remain identical to the Pixel 11 family while vertical pixel counts drop by 24 to 40 pixels. Rather than signaling lower display quality, display analysts note that minor vertical trims typically point to subtle aspect-ratio adjustments, slightly squarer corner radii, or reworked bezel proportions.

By contrast, the Pixel 12 Pro Fold receives a substantial sharpness upgrade. Jumping from 2,076 × 2,152 to 2,296 × 2,404 increases total inner-screen pixel count by roughly 24%—directly addressing text crispness and fine detail on an ~8-inch folding canvas.

At 2,296 × 2,404 pixels, the rumored Pixel 12 Pro Fold retains a near-square aspect ratio rather than pivoting toward wider, passport-style folding formats seen on rival devices. Keeping that square-leaning canvas preserves Google’s familiar cover-screen ergonomics when closed while offering a balanced layout for side-by-side split-screen apps, document reading, and web browsing when unfolded.

Separate supply-chain chatter also indicates Google is exploring Dual-UTG (Ultra-Thin Glass) inner display panels—placing protective glass layers both above and below the OLED stack—to reduce crease visibility and improve long-term folding durability. However, outer screen dimensions, peak brightness figures, and exterior chassis renders have not yet surfaced.

Because GSMA database entries only confirm model identifiers and baseline screen resolutions, several major hardware pillars remain unverified:

According to early prototype reports, Google is already testing Pixel 12 hardware on early builds of Android 18 ahead of an expected August 2027 Made by Google launch event—aligning with the late-summer release cadence established by the Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 families.

As development moves from early database registrations into hardware validation over the coming months, additional leaks around CAD renders, camera sensors, and Tensor G7 benchmarks will clarify how big a leap the Pixel 12 lineup represents. If you play on a Steam Deck or Steam Machine, the new Valve SteamOS 3.10 Preview brings a long list of changes you can try before they reach the stable release. Valve’s release notes add HDMI 2.1 support for AMD graphics, smoother variable refresh rate behavior and HDR and brightness control for the ROG Xbox Ally X20, while Deck Ready has been testing the update on Steam hardware. Preview builds can bring bugs, but you can see what has changed, what you need for the display improvements and how to switch channels.

SteamOS 3.10.1 is a Preview channel build that follows the 3.9 stable release and may contain bugs or stability issues. AMD graphics gain HDMI 2.1 support for VRR, FRL and ALLM, which Deck Ready reports brings 4K at 120 Hz to Steam Machine. Frame timing improves when the framerate limiter is used with VRR, alongside less flicker and smoother cursor movement. The ASUS ROG Xbox Ally X20 gains HDR and brightness adjustment in Game Mode. Version 3.10.1 fixes launch failures in the Forza Horizon series and an “invalid signal” error on certain displays.

SteamOS 3.10.1 is the current build on the Preview channel, where Valve tests features before they reach everyone. It follows the 3.9 stable release, and Valve describes it as an early build that may contain unexpected bugs or stability issues. SteamOS runs on Steam Deck and Steam Machine, and you can also install it on other PCs.

To try it, open Settings, then System, and change the System Update Channel to Preview.

The headline change is for AMD graphics, which gain HDMI 2.1 support for three features:

Deck Ready reports that this is what brings 4K at 120 Hz to Steam Machine, whose HDMI 2.1 support was missing at launch because of a licensing issue. You could already play at 120 FPS, but with some latency. The same support should reach other SteamOS PCs with AMD graphics, such as one with a 9070 XT.

To use it you need a compatible TV, the correct HDMI port on that TV and an HDMI 2.1 cable. The cable supplied with a PS5 is suitable, while a first-generation Nintendo Switch cable is not.

Become an expert in SteamOS and Steam Machine with the help of our in-depth articles and helpful guides.

Variable refresh rate matches the display’s refresh rate to the game’s frame rate as it changes, so a brief drop from 60 FPS to 55 looks smoother, although it does not remove the dip itself. This build tidies up how SteamOS behaves with it switched on.

Frame timing is improved when you use the framerate limiter with VRR, and the screen flickers less while you move around the Steam interface or leave it idle. Cursor movement now matches the game’s frame rate above 30 FPS, instead of spiking the panel to its maximum refresh rate.

In Deck Ready’s testing the frame-timing change made only a small difference, although that was mainly with older games that had no problems to begin with.

Game Mode adds HDR and brightness adjustment for the ASUS ROG Xbox Ally X20. People installing SteamOS on the handheld have also run into controls and speakers that do not work, so it is still early days for SteamOS on this hardware.

Version 3.10.1 itself is a small follow-up that repairs two problems introduced by 3.10: launch failures in titles such as the Forza Horizon series, and certain displays showing an “invalid signal” error. The wider 3.10 release also fixes:

NVIDIA graphics get general stability and performance improvements, support for mesh shaders on Turing and newer cards, and fixes for rendering corruption in Shadow of the Tomb Raider and The Surge 2.

Underneath, the Arch Linux base is updated, the kernel moves to Linux 7.3 and Desktop Mode goes from Plasma 6.7.3 to Plasma 6.8.2. Game Mode adds support for VK_EXT_present_timing, and Valve also lists many security and stability improvements, along with new timezone data for Cuba and for Canada’s Northwest Territories and Manitoba.

If you want the display improvements now, switch to the Preview channel, and check your TV, port and cable first if you are after 4K at 120 Hz on Steam Machine. Anyone who would rather avoid bugs can stay on the stable release, and Valve asks those who do hit a problem on Preview to report it on the SteamOS issue tracker.

FRL: Fixed Rate Link, the higher-bandwidth signal mode HDMI 2.1 uses. ALLM: Auto Low Latency Mode, which switches a TV to its low-lag game mode automatically. Samsung is set to reshape the smartphone landscape with its rollable smartphone concept, potentially named the Galaxy Z Slide or Galaxy Z Roll (following earlier “Galaxy Zoll” trademark filings). This innovative device is expected to feature a rollable display mechanism, allowing users to switch effortlessly between a compact form and a larger screen. By moving beyond traditional foldable designs, Samsung aims to provide a more versatile and immersive user experience without a central folding crease. However, this ambitious design introduces challenges such as durability, battery efficiency, and mechanical complexity, which Samsung must address to ensure the device’s success.

Motorized Crease-Free Expansion: Unspools a flexible OLED panel smoothly from inside the chassis—eliminating the physical hinge and visible screen crease of traditional foldables. Reinforced Guide Rails & Dynamic UI: Patent filings detail internal support slats and guide rails to keep the unrolled screen rigid while One UI scales app layouts on the fly. Silicon-Carbon Battery Tech: Rumored to adopt high-density silicon-carbon cells to preserve multi-hour endurance despite the space occupied by internal motors. 2027 Lineup Expansion: Tipped to join Samsung’s broader 2027 Galaxy Z family alongside the Galaxy Z Fold 9 and TriFold 2, though final naming and specs remain unconfirmed.

The Galaxy Z Slide is envisioned as a compact smartphone with a rollable display that expands smoothly on demand (with recent patents exploring both horizontal widening and vertical aspect-ratio extensions from 16:9 to 21:9). Unlike foldable devices, the flexible screen coils neatly inside the phone’s body and extends outward using a motorized sliding mechanism. This eliminates the need for a central hinge, avoiding the crease commonly associated with foldable screens and delivering a smoother, more uniform display.

To ensure durability, Samsung’s patent schematics incorporate reinforced guide rails and interlocking slat supports that back the rollable display during use. These features are designed to maintain the screen’s flatness and structural stability against finger pressure despite frequent sliding and rolling. Additionally, the Galaxy Z Slide is expected to feature a dynamic interface that adapts seamlessly to the degree of screen expansion, offering a smooth transition between compact and expanded modes.

This design not only enhances usability but also introduces a new level of practicality. The absence of a hinge and the integration of a motorized rollable mechanism represent a significant departure from conventional smartphone designs, positioning the Galaxy Z Slide as a compelling next step beyond dual-screen foldables.

The rollable design of the Galaxy Z Slide introduces a range of practical applications that could transform how users interact with their devices. In its retracted form, the device remains highly portable, easily fitting into pockets or small bags while looking much like a conventional handset. When expanded, the larger display unlocks an expansive canvas, ideal for multitasking, gaming and media consumption.

For example, users could watch a video on one side of the screen while browsing the web or taking notes on the other—without needing to open a clamshell or book-style hinge. The flexible interface ensures that apps and content automatically reflow to match the expanded screen dimensions, providing an optimized viewing experience. Whether for work, entertainment, or communication, the Galaxy Z Slide is designed to adapt to your needs, offering a level of versatility that fixed-screen smartphones cannot match.

This adaptability makes the device particularly appealing to professionals who require multitasking capabilities, as well as casual users seeking an enhanced media experience. By combining single-screen pocketability with on-demand display expansion, the Galaxy Z Slide could redefine the role of smartphones in daily life.

Samsung’s rollable smartphone concept incorporates several advanced technologies to address the unique demands of this design. These innovations are critical to making sure the device’s functionality, durability and efficiency:

These technological advancements highlight Samsung’s commitment to overcoming the engineering hurdles associated with rollable displays. By addressing issues such as rigidity, battery density and mechanical precision, Samsung is paving the way for a more reliable and efficient device.

While the Galaxy Z Slide concept is promising, it faces several hurdles before reaching mainstream shelves. Durability and ingress protection remain primary concerns, as repeated rolling cycles and sliding seams must keep out dust and lint over years of everyday pocket use. Samsung’s use of reinforced guide rails and tight chassis seals aims to mitigate this issue, but real-world longevity remains a key test.

Another significant challenge is the limited internal space for components such as the battery and cooling hardware. Housing a motorized sliding drive and coiled OLED drum reduces the room available for a conventional lithium-ion cell, making high-density silicon-carbon battery integration crucial to avoiding short runtimes.

The mechanical complexity of the motorized drive also introduces potential points of wear and higher manufacturing costs. Making sure the sliding mechanism operates quietly, smoothly, and reliably under varied temperatures and accidental drops will determine whether the Galaxy Z Slide can transition smoothly from showcase prototype to everyday flagship.

Samsung has been developing rollable screen technology for years—showcasing working sliding display prototypes at trade events like MWC 2026 while steadily filing patents covering motorized rails, traveling camera modules, and trademarks like “Galaxy Z Roll” and “Galaxy Zoll”. Supply-chain leaks suggest Samsung could expand its foldable portfolio in 2027 to include a commercial rollable model alongside the Galaxy Z Fold 9 and TriFold 2, though Samsung has not yet officially confirmed final naming, specs, or a launch date.

If brought to market successfully, the Galaxy Z Slide could represent a major leap forward in mobile form factors, delivering large-screen productivity in a sleek, crease-free body. Rather than replacing foldables overnight, a rollable Galaxy Z device would give enthusiasts an intriguing third path alongside flip and book-style phones—signaling the next chapter in flexible display innovation.

Google Gemini lets you build small apps, turn emails into tasks and work with files by describing what you need. Google Gemini is an AI chat app with a choice of models, thinking levels and custom instructions called skills, as well as a task mode that can work across Google services. Your AI Workflow found that Gemini could create a quote calculator, record incoming leads and draft replies for review. Take a closer look at how to use these options, along with video generation from images and a prompt.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen replaces Flash for quicker tasks, while Argon targets complex work and Carbon is intended for the most complex tasks. Hydrogen built a cleaning-business quote calculator in 30 seconds using medium thinking. Task mode added two matching email leads to a Google Sheet and saved reply drafts in Gmail. Argon processed five videos containing about an hour of footage and produced a milestone document in about five minutes. Omni 1.2 generated a 10-second teaser from reference images, with dialogue matching the prompt word for word.

Google Gemini combines a chat interface with tools for creating apps, working with files and carrying out tasks across Google services. Its model menu includes replacements and additions for different types of work.

Your model selection determines how Gemini approaches a request, while a separate thinking-level control offers low, medium and high settings. Gemini can also use custom instructions, called skills, when a task calls for them.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen replaces Gemini Flash and is intended for quicker tasks. Hydrogen is faster and hallucinates less than its predecessor.

Gemini 4 Argon is aimed at more complex work, including code and analysis, while Gemini 4 Carbon is intended for the most complex tasks. Your AI Workflow recommends Argon for processing large amounts of data and producing an output, but considers it less suited to creative work than Hydrogen.

You can describe a small app in a Gemini prompt, including its inputs and the result it should produce. With Hydrogen set to medium thinking, a request for a cleaning-business quote calculator produced an app in 30 seconds.

The request specified a $40 hourly rate, prices for extras and a 10% returning-client discount. The calculator accepted a five-hour booking, add-ons and the discount, then displayed a total and a client message that could be copied into WhatsApp.

Use Share to copy a link that someone can open to use the calculator. Anyone with the link can also see the app’s contents, so Your AI Workflow warns against including sensitive data.

Check out more relevant guides from our extensive collection on Google Gemini 4 models that you might find useful.

Task mode can respond to incoming messages according to instructions in a prompt. For lead collection, you can ask Gemini to watch for “quote” or “inquiry” in an email subject and record the sender’s name, company, request and budget in a Google Sheet.

The automation is meant to check Google Calendar for two open times during the rest of the week and save a Gmail reply offering them, rather than sending it. When Gemini noticed that the leads sheet did not exist, it created an empty one on request. You can view and edit files inside Gemini.

After two matching quote requests arrived, the chat added both clients as rows in the sheet and saved reply drafts in Gmail. One draft offered two available times and could be edited or sent directly.

Task mode can also carry out a step-by-step request using material you add from Google Drive. You can select Argon and attach a project folder for Gemini to process before it creates an output.

For a milestone breakdown, Argon processed five videos containing about an hour of footage and produced a document in about five minutes. It included a summary, a table of milestones and dates, links to recordings and a detailed feature breakdown. A check against the footage confirmed details that had initially raised concerns about hallucination.

The document opens like a Google Doc, and you can share it in the same way, including by changing access to anyone with the link.

Skills are custom instructions for particular tasks that you can create directly in a Gemini chat. To request an email-responder skill, you can ask Gemini to analyse the previous two weeks of emails and identify what to say, when to say it and the writer’s style.

A resulting skill specifies when to use it, and Gemini can automatically load a relevant skill without a separate reminder. In a task for sponsored-video or partnership messages, Gemini loaded the email-responder skill and drafted a reply in the requested style with the correct details for review.

That automation needs keywords to identify the messages; it will not work with every email. You can then review and send the draft rather than having it dispatched automatically.

Omni 1.2 is a video model that accepts reference images alongside a text prompt. It is intended to follow reference images and instructions closely and recreate requested dialogue.

A request using separate hoodie and logo images produced a 10-second launch teaser whose dialogue followed the prompt word for word. One detail did not match the scene: the person asking about the hoodie never looked at it, making the question less clear. Your AI Workflow suggests that might be fixable through chat.

Start by choosing a model for the work: Hydrogen is intended for quicker requests, while Argon is aimed at more complex tasks. You can share an app with a link, but leave out sensitive information because anyone with the link can see its contents. For anyone using Google Gemini to build a small app, begin with a prompt describing its inputs and the result you want.

Apple has not announced an iPhone 20 or confirmed whether it will skip the iPhone 19 name, yet supply-chain leaks point to a major 20th-anniversary flagship expected in September 2027. Internally linked to codenames like “Glasswing” and Pro/Pro Max development lines (V73 and V74), current rumors focus on quad-curved glass, COE OLED displays, and silicon-anode battery cells. Quad-Curved Glass & Prototype Testing: Leaks point to a glass-heavy chassis with 3D quad-curved edges and roughly ~1mm borders in testing alongside flat-glass prototypes. Rumors around the 20th-anniversary iPhone center on a glass-forward chassis that curves around all four edges and corners, framed by a slim metal mid-band. Leak chatter indicates Apple is currently testing multiple prototypes—including quad-curved and flat-glass variants—while refining edge curvature and shrinking visible borders toward roughly 1mm.

While a completely uninterrupted front display remains an engineering hurdle for 2027, recent component leaks suggest a smaller front cutout than today’s models while retaining a raised rear camera plateau.

Supply-chain reports indicate Apple is exploring COE (Color Filter on Encapsulation) OLED panels for the 2027 Pro lineup. By removing the traditional polarizer layer and integrating color filters directly onto the encapsulation layer, COE OLED can reduce panel thickness while improving brightness and power efficiency—though some supply-chain analysts caution that polarizer-free panels face tight manufacturing yields.

Display sizes are also tipped to edge upward for the first time since 2024, with the smaller Pro model growing from 6.27 inches to roughly 6.41 inches and the Pro Max expanding from 6.86 inches to 6.96 inches.

The new NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X can run Fallout 4 at 4K, but Elden Ring falls short of 60 fps at 1440p even on medium settings. This 140W desktop chip is aimed at AI work, yet its ARM CPU and Blackwell graphics also let you play games on a compact Windows workstation. Shared memory and Windows translation bring trade-offs, while DLSS and frame generation can improve results in some games. Find out what ETA Prime reports about gaming performance and how those trade-offs affect the games you play.

The New RTX Spark N1X workstation has 20 ARM cores, 6,144 CUDA cores, 128GB of unified memory and a 140W desktop TDP. Its approximately 300GB/s memory bandwidth is lower than the RTX 5070’s 672GB/s, and Prism translation adds overhead. The N1X scored around 14,086 in 3DMark Time Spy, ahead of RTX 5070 and RTX 5060 laptop averages. Gaming results varied: Fallout 4 held 60 fps at 4K ultra, while Elden Ring fell short of 60 fps at 1440p medium. Gears of War: E-Day averaged 46 fps without frame generation and 79 fps with it, using ultra settings and DLSS quality.

The RTX Spark N1X can run games on the MSI Edge Mesa NAI Plus, a small-form-factor workstation aimed more at AI work than gaming. The chip combines an ARM CPU and NVIDIA Blackwell graphics, with unified memory shared between the CPU and GPU rather than separate pools of system and graphics memory. It runs Windows with help from Microsoft’s Prism translation layer.

The desktop chip has more power headroom than the 20-core N1X laptops seen so far, allowing higher CPU and GPU clocks, but its memory bandwidth is lower than that of an RTX 5060 or RTX 5070. The workstation’s main specifications are:

In the tested system, memory was split evenly, with 64GB for Windows and 64GB for the GPU. In FurMark, the GPU drew close to 115 watts, while the CPU has been observed drawing from 51 to 68 watts. N1X laptops seen so far have generally reached around 85 watts, with some boosting to around 90 watts.

At 672GB per second, the RTX 5070 has higher memory bandwidth, while the N1X also has overhead from Prism translation. Extra power headroom should give the desktop variant much better performance than the laptop version, though that remains an expectation.

Discover other guides from our vast content that could be of interest on RTX Spark N1X and Blackwell.

In synthetic benchmarks, the N1X scored ahead of RTX 5070 and RTX 5060 laptop averages, although those scores do not tell the whole story of game performance. At 140W, it scored around 14,086 in 3DMark Time Spy and 3,453 in 3DMark Steel Nomad.

Driver updates and further Prism work may improve performance, but the game results below show what the workstation delivered with its current software.

The workstation handled the esports games tested without frame generation, although Marvel Rivals was weaker than the other two results. Fortnite and Marvel Rivals used DLSS on its quality setting, and DLSS is likely to be useful for many of the games tested at 1440p.

The latest Fallout 4 update ran at a continuous 60 fps at 4K ultra, making older games a good fit for higher-resolution play. Left 4 Dead and Half-Life can also run with settings maxed out at 4K, while Street Fighter 5 and Injustice are expected to perform well at 4K ultra.

Elden Ring struggled to reach 60 fps at 1440p high, and reducing the settings to medium still left it short of that mark. At 1080p, it reached 60 fps on high settings and around 51 fps with settings maxed out.

Mortal Kombat 1 averaged around 51 fps at very high settings without DLSS. Dropping to high at 1440p, still without DLSS, produced a decent result, although ETA Prime notes that the game felt odd for a reason that was difficult to pinpoint.

DLSS made a difference in demanding titles, though the benefit varied by game. Ghost of Tsushima remained fully playable at 1440p ultra without DLSS or other scaling. Spider-Man 2 performed poorly without DLSS, but ran better than expected at 1440p high with DLSS quality and NVIDIA’s RTX Spark Game Ready driver.

Japanese Drift Master ran at 1440p ultra with DLSS set to balanced, while turning DLSS off at 1440p sent it into the low 40s fps. Hogwarts Legacy used DLSS frame generation at 1440p ultra, without multi-frame generation, which is also available on the chip.

Gears of War: E-Day gave the clearest frame-generation comparison: its built-in benchmark averaged 46 fps without frame generation and 79 fps with it, using the ultra preset and DLSS quality in both runs.

ETA Prime sees the MSI Edge Mesa NAI Plus as an AI workstation that handles its main job well while also letting you play games. It was not designed specifically for gaming, and results vary for players who prefer to avoid frame generation. Elden Ring reached 60 fps at 1080p high but fell short at 1440p, even on medium settings.

Daerah dengan Potensi Hujan Lebat di Jabodetabek, Bogor Waspada

Warga menggunakan payung berjalan saat hujan lebat di JPO Mampang, Jakarta. Bloomberg Technoz/Andrean Kristianto

Bloomberg Technoz, Jakarta - Badan Meteorologi, Klimatologi, dan Geofisika (BMKG) memperingatkan potensi hujan dengan intensitas sedang hingga lebat di sejumlah wilayah Jabodetabek pada 23 November 2026. Kabupaten dan Kota Bogor menjadi wilayah yang perlu diwaspadai karena berpotensi mengalami hujan sedang hingga lebat pada siang sampai sore hari.

BMKG melalui prakiraan cuaca wilayah Jabodetabek yang diperbarui pada Senin (23/11/2026) pukul 07.00 WIB menyebutkan, kondisi cuaca pada pagi hari secara umum berawan hingga berawan tebal.
